text: What is binomial nomenclature? Give two rules followed in writing a scientific name.
modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of naming every organism with two words: the generic name followed by the specific epithet (e.g. Panthera leo). Rules: (i) names are in Latin or Latinised and are printed in italics, or underlined separately when handwritten; (ii) the genus begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter; the name of the author may be added in abbreviated form after the epithet.

text: Differentiate between a herbarium and a botanical garden.
modelAnswer: A herbarium is a store-house of dried, pressed and preserved plant specimens mounted on sheets with labels, serving as a quick reference for identification. A botanical garden is a place where living plants are grown and maintained for identification and study, each plant being labelled with its scientific name and family (e.g. Kew in England, Indian Botanical Garden at Howrah).
keyPoints: Herbarium: dried, pressed specimens on sheets
Both are taxonomic aids for identification

text: Explain why metabolism and consciousness are considered defining properties of living organisms, whereas growth and reproduction are not.
modelAnswer: Metabolism – the sum of all chemical reactions occurring in the body – is found in every living organism and in no non-living object, so it is a defining property. Consciousness – the ability to sense the surroundings and respond – is likewise shown by all organisms, from prokaryotes to plants and animals. Growth, however, is also seen in non-living things that grow by surface accumulation (crystals, mountains), and reproduction is absent in some living individuals such as mules, worker bees and infertile couples. Hence growth and reproduction are not all-inclusive defining features.
keyPoints: Metabolism present in all living things, absent in non-living
Consciousness: all organisms sense and respond

text: What are taxonomic categories? Arrange the following in ascending order: class, species, kingdom, family, genus, order, phylum.
modelAnswer: Taxonomic categories are the ranks or levels in the hierarchy of classification; each category (taxon when it refers to an actual group of organisms) represents a rank. Ascending order: species → genus → family → order → class → phylum (division in plants) → kingdom. As we go higher, the number of organisms included increases and the number of shared characters decreases.
keyPoints: Higher category: more organisms, fewer common characters

text: Describe the various taxonomical aids that help in the identification and study of organisms.
modelAnswer: (i) Herbarium – dried, pressed plant specimens on sheets with labels on name, place, date, collector; quick reference. (ii) Botanical gardens – living plants grown and labelled (Kew, England; Howrah, India). (iii) Museums – preserved plants and animals, in jars with preservative or as dry/stuffed specimens, insects in boxes, skeletons. (iv) Zoological parks – wild animals kept in protected environments close to natural habitats, allowing study of behaviour. (v) Keys – analytical tools based on contrasting couplets of characters, used for identifying families, genera and species. Other aids include flora, manuals, monographs and catalogues, which give descriptions and help identification.

text: Why is classification of living organisms necessary?
modelAnswer: Millions of organisms exist, and studying each individually is impossible. Classification groups organisms on the basis of similarities and differences, making study easier, helping identification, showing evolutionary relationships among groups, and giving a universal system of reference understood by scientists everywhere.
keyPoints: Huge diversity cannot be studied individually

text: Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker's classification and state any two criteria he used.
modelAnswer: Kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Criteria used: cell structure (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), body (thallus) organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships (any two).

text: Distinguish between viruses and viroids. Name a disease caused by each.
modelAnswer: Viruses are non-cellular infectious particles consisting of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid); they are inert outside a host cell and become active inside it. Example: TMV causes tobacco mosaic; influenza, AIDS and mumps in humans. Viroids are smaller, consisting only of a free low-molecular-weight RNA without a protein coat. Example: potato spindle tuber disease.

text: Describe the structure of a lichen and state its ecological significance.
modelAnswer: A lichen is a symbiotic association between an alga (phycobiont, usually a green alga or cyanobacterium) and a fungus (mycobiont). The alga prepares food by photosynthesis; the fungus provides shelter and absorbs water and mineral nutrients. They are so closely associated that a lichen looks like a single organism. Significance: lichens are pioneer colonisers of bare rock, help in soil formation, and are very good indicators of air pollution because they do not grow in polluted areas (SO₂-sensitive).

text: Compare the four classes of fungi with respect to mycelium, asexual spores, sexual spores and examples.
modelAnswer: Phycomycetes: mycelium aseptate, coenocytic; asexual spores – zoospores (motile) or aplanospores (non-motile) formed endogenously in sporangia; sexual spores – zygospores by fusion of gametes; examples Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo. Ascomycetes (sac fungi): mycelium branched, septate; asexual spores – conidia formed exogenously on conidiophores; sexual spores – ascospores inside asci, often in fruiting bodies called ascocarps; examples Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora, yeast (unicellular). Basidiomycetes: mycelium branched, septate; asexual spores generally absent, vegetative reproduction by fragmentation; sexual spores – basidiospores produced exogenously on basidia in basidiocarps; examples Agaricus, Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust). Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi): mycelium septate, branched; asexual spores – conidia; sexual phase not known; examples Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma.

text: Why are cyanobacteria considered important in paddy fields?
modelAnswer: Many cyanobacteria (e.g. Nostoc, Anabaena) possess heterocysts that fix atmospheric nitrogen. Growing in waterlogged paddy fields, they add fixed nitrogen to the soil, acting as natural biofertilisers and increasing rice yield.

text: Give three distinguishing features of Archaebacteria and name their three groups.
modelAnswer: Archaebacteria live in extreme habitats (hot springs, salty areas, marshes); their cell wall lacks peptidoglycan and has a structure different from eubacteria; their membrane lipids are branched (ether-linked), aiding survival in harsh conditions. Groups: halophiles (salty areas), thermoacidophiles (hot springs) and methanogens (marshy areas, gut of ruminants; produce methane).

text: Name the three classes of algae and give the stored food in each.
modelAnswer: Chlorophyceae (green algae) – starch (also oil droplets); Phaeophyceae (brown algae) – laminarin or mannitol; Rhodophyceae (red algae) – floridean starch.

text: Explain alternation of generations with reference to a moss.
modelAnswer: In a moss the main plant body is the haploid gametophyte, which first appears as a filamentous protonema and then as an upright leafy stage bearing antheridia and archegonia. Antherozoids swim through water to the archegonium and fuse with the egg to form a diploid zygote. The zygote grows into a sporophyte (foot, seta and capsule) that remains attached to and dependent on the gametophyte. Spore mother cells in the capsule divide by meiosis to form haploid spores, which germinate into new protonemata. Thus haploid gametophytic and diploid sporophytic generations alternate.

text: Give three differences between gymnosperms and angiosperms.
modelAnswer: (i) Gymnosperms have naked ovules and seeds; in angiosperms ovules are enclosed in an ovary and seeds in fruits. (ii) Gymnosperms lack flowers and bear cones (strobili); angiosperms bear flowers. (iii) Gymnosperms show single fertilisation and haploid endosperm formed before fertilisation; angiosperms show double fertilisation with triploid endosperm. (Also: xylem vessels usually absent in gymnosperms; companion cells absent in gymnosperm phloem.)
keyPoints: Single vs double fertilisation; haploid vs triploid endosperm

text: Describe the three types of life cycle patterns found in plants with suitable examples, and state the stage at which meiosis occurs in each.
modelAnswer: (1) Haplontic: the dominant, free-living, photosynthetic phase is the haploid gametophyte; the sporophyte is represented only by the single-celled zygote, which undergoes meiosis to form haploid spores (zygotic meiosis). Examples: Volvox, Spirogyra, some Chlamydomonas. (2) Diplontic: the diploid sporophyte is dominant, independent and photosynthetic; the gametophyte is reduced to a few cells (pollen grain and embryo sac). Meiosis occurs in spore mother cells to form spores (sporic meiosis). Examples: gymnosperms and angiosperms; among algae, Fucus. (3) Haplo-diplontic: both phases are multicellular. In bryophytes the haploid gametophyte is dominant and the short-lived sporophyte depends on it; in pteridophytes the diploid sporophyte is dominant and the gametophyte (prothallus) is free-living but short-lived. Meiosis occurs in spore mother cells. Examples: bryophytes, pteridophytes; algae such as Ectocarpus, Polysiphonia, kelps.
keyPoints: Haplontic: gametophyte dominant, zygotic meiosis, Volvox/Spirogyra
Diplontic: sporophyte dominant, seed plants, Fucus

text: What is heterospory? Why is it considered a precursor to the seed habit?
modelAnswer: Heterospory is the production of two kinds of spores – small microspores and large megaspores – as in Selaginella and Salvinia. The megaspore is retained and develops into the female gametophyte on the parent sporophyte; this retention, with development of the embryo inside, is an important step towards the formation of seeds.

text: State two economic uses each of red algae and brown algae.
modelAnswer: Red algae: agar from Gelidium and Gracilaria (culture media, ice-cream, jellies); carrageen as stabiliser; Porphyra eaten as food. Brown algae: algin used as a thickener and in ice-creams; kelps like Laminaria are a source of iodine and used as food.

text: Distinguish between diploblastic and triploblastic animals with one example each.
modelAnswer: Diploblastic animals have cells arranged in two embryonic layers – an outer ectoderm and an inner endoderm, with an undifferentiated mesoglea between them (e.g. Hydra, coelenterates). Triploblastic animals develop a third layer, mesoderm, between ectoderm and endoderm (e.g. flatworms to chordates, such as earthworm).

text: Explain the terms acoelomate, pseudocoelomate and coelomate with an example of each.
modelAnswer: Coelom is the body cavity lined by mesoderm. Acoelomates lack a body cavity (e.g. Platyhelminthes – Taenia, Fasciola). Pseudocoelomates have a body cavity that is not fully lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm (e.g. Aschelminthes – Ascaris). Coelomates have a true coelom lined by mesoderm on both sides (e.g. Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Chordata).

text: List the distinguishing features of class Aves and class Mammalia (any four each), with two examples of each class.
modelAnswer: Aves: body covered with feathers; forelimbs modified into wings; beak present, no teeth; pneumatic (hollow) bones; four-chambered heart; homoiothermous; oviparous with direct development; skin dry without glands except the oil gland at the tail base; crop and gizzard in the digestive tract. Examples: Columba (pigeon), Corvus (crow), Psittacula (parrot), Pavo (peacock). Mammalia: mammary glands produce milk; hair on the skin; external ears (pinnae); different types of teeth (heterodont); four-chambered heart; homoiothermous; lungs for respiration; mostly viviparous. Examples: Ornithorhynchus (oviparous), Macropus, Pteropus, Balaenoptera, Felis, Canis, Homo.

text: Write three features of phylum Arthropoda and name one insect vector of disease.
modelAnswer: Arthropods have jointed appendages; their body is covered by a chitinous exoskeleton and divided into head, thorax and abdomen; they have an open circulatory system; respiration is by gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae; excretion is through Malpighian tubules; sense organs include compound eyes, antennae and statocysts. Vector example: Anopheles (malaria), Culex (filariasis) or Aedes (dengue).

text: Why are hemichordates now placed as a separate phylum and not as a sub-phylum of Chordata?
modelAnswer: Hemichordates (e.g. Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus) have a rudimentary rod-like structure called the stomochord in the collar region, which was earlier thought to be a notochord. It is now considered not homologous to the notochord, so hemichordates are placed as a separate phylum among non-chordates.

text: What is metagenesis? Name the phylum in which it occurs.
modelAnswer: Metagenesis is alternation of generations between the asexual polyp form, which produces medusae by budding, and the sexual medusa form, which produces polyps through gametes. It occurs in some members of Cnidaria (Coelenterata), e.g. Obelia.

text: Give two examples each of roots modified for (a) storage of food and (b) respiration.
modelAnswer: (a) Storage: carrot (tap root), turnip, sweet potato (adventitious root), radish. (b) Respiration: pneumatophores of Rhizophora and other mangroves growing in swampy areas.

text: Define placentation. Describe any three types with an example of each.
modelAnswer: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary. Marginal – placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and ovules are borne on it in two rows (pea). Axile – placenta is axial in a multilocular ovary and ovules are attached to it (china rose, tomato, lemon). Parietal – ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on the peripheral part; the ovary becomes two-chambered by a false septum (mustard, Argemone). Free central – ovules borne on a central axis without septa (Dianthus, Primrose). Basal – placenta at the base of the ovary with a single ovule (sunflower, marigold).

text: Describe the floral characteristics of the family Fabaceae. Write its floral formula and give two economically important plants.
modelAnswer: Fabaceae (Papilionoideae of Leguminosae): Inflorescence racemose. Flower bisexual, zygomorphic. Calyx – five sepals, gamosepalous, imbricate aestivation. Corolla – five petals, polypetalous, papilionaceous: one posterior large standard (vexillum), two lateral wings, two anterior petals forming the keel enclosing stamens and pistil; vexillary aestivation. Androecium – ten stamens, diadelphous (9)+1, anthers dithecous. Gynoecium – ovary superior, monocarpellary, unilocular with many ovules, marginal placentation; style single. Fruit – legume (pod); seeds non-endospermic. Floral formula: % ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₁₊₂₊₍₂₎ A₍₉₎₊₁ G̲₁. Economic importance: pulses (gram, arhar, moong, soybean – protein), edible oil (soybean, groundnut), dye (indigo), fibres (sunhemp), fodder (Sesbania, Trifolium), ornamentals (lupin, sweet pea), medicine (Muliathi).

text: Distinguish between racemose and cymose inflorescence.
modelAnswer: Racemose: the main axis continues to grow indefinitely; flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession (older flowers at base, younger at apex); e.g. mustard, radish. Cymose: the main axis terminates in a flower and so has limited growth; flowers are borne in basipetal order (oldest flower at the tip); e.g. jasmine, Solanum species.

text: What is aestivation? Name the types of aestivation found in calotropis and china rose.
modelAnswer: Aestivation is the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in the floral bud with respect to other members of the same whorl. Calotropis shows valvate aestivation (margins just touch without overlap). China rose shows twisted aestivation (one margin of each appendage overlaps the next).

text: Describe three stem modifications for vegetative propagation with examples.
modelAnswer: Runner – a slender lateral branch arising from the base and running aerially along the ground, rooting at nodes (grasses, strawberry). Stolon – a slender lateral branch arising from the base, growing aerially, then arching downwards to touch the ground (mint, jasmine). Offset – a short internode lateral branch with a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots, found in aquatic plants (Pistia, Eichhornia). Sucker – lateral branch from the underground base of the main stem, growing obliquely upward to form leafy shoots (banana, pineapple, Chrysanthemum).
keyPoints: Each gives rise to new plants

text: What are meristems? Name the three types based on position.
modelAnswer: Meristems are regions of actively dividing cells responsible for growth in plants. By position: apical meristems (at root and shoot tips, increase length), intercalary meristems (at the base of leaves and internodes, e.g. grasses) and lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium, increase girth).

text: Give three differences between a dicot root and a monocot root in transverse section.
modelAnswer: (i) Xylem bundles: dicot root has 2–4 (diarch to tetrarch); monocot root more than six (polyarch). (ii) Pith: small or absent in dicot root; large and well developed in monocot root. (iii) Secondary growth: occurs in dicot roots (vascular cambium forms from conjunctive tissue and pericycle); absent in monocot roots.

text: Describe the process of secondary growth in a dicot stem.
modelAnswer: Vascular cambium: In a young dicot stem the intrafascicular cambium lies between primary xylem and phloem. Medullary ray cells adjoining it become meristematic to form the interfascicular cambium, producing a continuous cambial ring. The ring cuts off cells on both sides – more towards the inside (secondary xylem) than towards the outside (secondary phloem). As secondary xylem accumulates, primary and secondary phloem are crushed. The cambium also forms narrow bands of parenchyma, the secondary medullary rays. Seasonal activity: in spring the cambium forms early wood with wide vessels; in winter it forms late wood with narrow vessels, giving annual rings. Cork cambium: As the stem thickens, the outer cortex and epidermis break and are replaced. The phellogen develops in the cortex and cuts off phellem (cork) outwards and phelloderm (secondary cortex) inwards; together they form periderm. Cork is impervious to water due to suberin. Lenticels form for gas exchange.
keyPoints: Secondary xylem inward, phloem outward (more xylem)

text: Distinguish between heartwood and sapwood.
modelAnswer: Heartwood (duramen) is the central, dark-coloured part of secondary xylem; its cells are dead, filled with tannins, resins, gums, oils and aromatic substances; it does not conduct water but gives mechanical support and is durable and resistant to microbes and insects. Sapwood (alburnum) is the peripheral, light-coloured region of secondary xylem; it conducts water and minerals from roots to leaves.

text: Distinguish between dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves.
modelAnswer: Dorsiventral (dicot) leaves have mesophyll differentiated into palisade parenchyma on the upper side and spongy parenchyma on the lower side; stomata are usually more numerous on the lower epidermis. Isobilateral (monocot) leaves have undifferentiated mesophyll, stomata on both surfaces and bulliform cells on the upper epidermis.

text: What are the components of phloem? Which component is absent in gymnosperms?
modelAnswer: Phloem in angiosperms consists of sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres (bast fibres). In gymnosperms sieve tubes and companion cells are absent; instead albuminous cells and sieve cells are present.
keyPoints: Companion cells/sieve tubes absent in gymnosperms

text: Differentiate between tendons and ligaments.
modelAnswer: Both are dense regular connective tissues with collagen fibres arranged in parallel rows. Tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones; ligaments attach one bone to another bone.

text: Compare skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.
modelAnswer: Skeletal muscle: attached to bones, fibres striated, unbranched, multinucleate, voluntary. Smooth muscle: found in walls of internal organs (blood vessels, stomach, intestine); fibres spindle-shaped (fusiform), non-striated, uninucleate, involuntary. Cardiac muscle: found only in the heart; fibres striated, branched, connected by intercalated discs that allow cells to contract as a unit; involuntary.

text: Name the three types of cell junctions found in animal tissues and state the function of each.
modelAnswer: Tight junctions help stop substances from leaking across a tissue. Adhering junctions perform cementing to keep neighbouring cells together. Gap junctions facilitate cells to communicate with each other by connecting the cytoplasm of adjoining cells, allowing rapid transfer of ions, small molecules and sometimes big molecules.

text: Describe the digestive system of the cockroach.
modelAnswer: The alimentary canal is divided into foregut, midgut and hindgut. Mouth opens into a short tubular pharynx leading to a narrow tubular oesophagus, which opens into a sac-like crop used for storing food. The crop is followed by the gizzard (proventriculus), which has an outer layer of thick circular muscles and a thick inner cuticle forming six chitinous plates called teeth, used for grinding food. The foregut is lined by cuticle. At the junction of foregut and midgut there is a ring of 6–8 blind tubules called hepatic or gastric caecae, which secrete digestive juice. The midgut (mesenteron) is the site of digestion and absorption. At the junction of midgut and hindgut is a ring of 100–150 yellow Malpighian tubules that remove nitrogenous wastes (uric acid). The hindgut is broader and is differentiated into ileum, colon and rectum, which opens out through the anus. Salivary glands open near the mouth.
keyPoints: Foregut parts and crop as storage

text: What is the function of Malpighian tubules in cockroach?
modelAnswer: Malpighian tubules, about 100–150 in number, lined by glandular and ciliated cells, absorb nitrogenous waste products and convert them into uric acid, which is excreted out through the hindgut. Cockroaches are therefore uricotelic.

text: Describe the circulatory system of the cockroach.
modelAnswer: The cockroach has an open circulatory system. Blood vessels are poorly developed and open into spaces (haemocoel). Visceral organs located in the haemocoel are bathed in blood (haemolymph), which is composed of colourless plasma and haemocytes. The heart is an elongated muscular tube lying along the mid-dorsal line of the thorax and abdomen, differentiated into funnel-shaped chambers with ostia on either side. Blood from sinuses enters the heart through ostia and is pumped anteriorly to sinuses again.

text: State the cell theory as modified by Rudolf Virchow.
modelAnswer: (i) All living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells. (ii) All cells arise from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula-e cellula). The original cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann did not explain how new cells form; Virchow added the second postulate.

text: Give three differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
modelAnswer: (i) Nucleus: prokaryotes lack a well-defined nucleus (genetic material is naked in a nucleoid); eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus. (ii) Organelles: membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, ER and Golgi are absent in prokaryotes and present in eukaryotes. (iii) Ribosomes: 70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotic cytoplasm. (iv) DNA: prokaryotes have a single circular chromosome and often plasmids; eukaryotes have linear chromosomes with histones.

text: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane and list its functions.
modelAnswer: Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972), the model states that the membrane is a quasi-fluid lipid bilayer, mainly of phospholipids arranged with polar heads facing outwards and non-polar hydrocarbon tails inwards. Cholesterol is also present. Proteins are of two types: peripheral proteins lying on the surface and integral proteins partially or totally buried in the membrane. The quasi-fluid nature allows lateral movement of proteins within the bilayer, measured as fluidity. Carbohydrates are attached to lipids and proteins (glycolipids and glycoproteins) on the outer surface. Functions: fluidity is important for cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division. The membrane is selectively permeable; it allows passive transport (diffusion, osmosis) of some molecules and active transport of others (e.g. Na⁺/K⁺ pump using ATP).

text: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion.
modelAnswer: A mitochondrion is a sausage-shaped or cylindrical organelle (0.2–1.0 µm diameter, 1.0–4.1 µm long) bounded by two membranes. The outer membrane forms the continuous limiting boundary. The inner membrane forms infoldings called cristae towards the matrix, which increase surface area and bear the enzymes of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase (F₀–F₁ particles). The space between membranes is the outer compartment; the inner compartment is filled with a dense homogeneous matrix containing Krebs cycle enzymes, a single circular DNA, a few RNA molecules and 70S ribosomes. Mitochondria divide by fission.

text: What are the functions of the Golgi apparatus?
modelAnswer: The Golgi apparatus packages materials to be delivered to intracellular targets or secreted outside the cell; proteins synthesised on the RER are modified in its cisternae before release from the trans (maturing) face. It is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids, and it gives rise to lysosomes.

text: What are centrioles? State their structure.
modelAnswer: Centrioles are a pair of cylindrical structures surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material, forming the centrosome. Each centriole has a cartwheel organisation of nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin protein, each fibril being a triplet. They form the basal bodies of cilia/flagella and give rise to spindle fibres during cell division in animal cells.

text: Distinguish between primary and secondary metabolites, with two examples of each.
modelAnswer: Primary metabolites have identifiable functions and play known roles in normal physiological processes, e.g. amino acids, sugars, nucleotides, fatty acids. Secondary metabolites have no obvious role in routine physiology of the producer, though many are useful to humans, e.g. alkaloids (morphine, codeine), flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics, coloured pigments, gums, lectins.

text: Describe the four levels of protein structure.
modelAnswer: Primary: the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain, from the N-terminal to the C-terminal, held by peptide bonds. Secondary: folding of the chain into regular shapes such as the right-handed α-helix or β-pleated sheet, stabilised by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary: further folding of the helical chain into a three-dimensional shape (like a hollow woollen ball), stabilised by hydrogen, ionic, disulphide and hydrophobic interactions; essential for many biological activities. Quaternary: the arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits with respect to each other, e.g. adult haemoglobin with two α and two β subunits.

text: Explain the mechanism of enzyme action and describe the factors that affect enzyme activity.
modelAnswer: Mechanism: The enzyme (E) has an active site, a crevice into which the substrate (S) fits. (i) The substrate binds to the active site, forming the enzyme–substrate complex (ES). (ii) Binding induces a change in enzyme shape so that it fits more tightly (induced fit). (iii) The active site brings bonds of the substrate into close proximity, forming an enzyme–product complex via a transition state of lower activation energy. (iv) The enzyme releases the products and the unchanged enzyme is free to bind another substrate: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P. Factors: Temperature – activity rises to an optimum and then falls as heat denatures the protein; low temperature only inactivates temporarily. pH – each enzyme has an optimum pH (pepsin ~2, trypsin ~8); deviation alters ionisation and shape. Substrate concentration – velocity rises with [S] until Vmax, when all active sites are saturated. Enzyme concentration – rate is proportional when substrate is in excess. Inhibitors – competitive inhibitors (malonate for succinic dehydrogenase) resemble the substrate; non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere.
keyPoints: Active site, ES complex, induced fit
Lowered activation energy, products released, enzyme unchanged

text: What are cofactors? Describe their three kinds with examples.
modelAnswer: Cofactors are non-protein constituents bound to an enzyme that make it catalytically active; the protein part is the apoenzyme. (i) Prosthetic groups – organic compounds tightly bound to the apoenzyme, e.g. haem in peroxidase and catalase. (ii) Coenzymes – organic compounds whose association with the apoenzyme is transient, usually during catalysis; many contain vitamins, e.g. NAD and NADP contain niacin. (iii) Metal ions – form coordination bonds with side chains at the active site and with the substrate, e.g. zinc for carboxypeptidase.

text: Name the six classes of enzymes according to the International Union of Biochemistry.
modelAnswer: (1) Oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases, (2) Transferases, (3) Hydrolases, (4) Lyases, (5) Isomerases, (6) Ligases.

text: Why is DNA called a polynucleotide? Name its building blocks.
modelAnswer: DNA is a long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides joined by 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds, hence a polynucleotide. Each nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base (adenine, guanine, cytosine or thymine), deoxyribose sugar and a phosphate group.

text: What is the G₀ phase? Give an example of cells that enter it.
modelAnswer: G₀ (quiescent stage) is the inactive stage entered by cells that exit the G₁ phase and do not divide further. Cells in G₀ remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless required. Example: heart cells and many neurons in adult animals.

text: Describe the events of the three phases of interphase.
modelAnswer: G₁ (Gap 1): the cell is metabolically active and grows continuously but does not replicate DNA; it prepares for DNA synthesis. S (synthesis): DNA replicates, so the amount of DNA per cell doubles (2C → 4C) though the chromosome number stays the same; in animal cells centrioles duplicate in the cytoplasm. G₂ (Gap 2): proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis while cell growth continues.
keyPoints: S DNA doubles, chromosome number same

text: Describe the substages of prophase I of meiosis.
modelAnswer: Prophase I is long and complex, divided into five substages. (1) Leptotene: chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope; compaction continues. (2) Zygotene: homologous chromosomes start pairing (synapsis), accompanied by formation of the synaptonemal complex; the complex of a pair of synapsed homologues is a bivalent or tetrad. (3) Pachytene: the four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct; recombination nodules appear and crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, mediated by the enzyme recombinase, leading to recombination of genetic material. (4) Diplotene: the synaptonemal complex dissolves and homologues tend to separate except at the sites of crossing over, the X-shaped chiasmata; this can last months or years in oocytes of some vertebrates. (5) Diakinesis: terminalisation of chiasmata; chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle is assembled; by the end the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down.

text: Give three differences between mitosis and meiosis.
modelAnswer: (i) Mitosis occurs in somatic cells (and in haploid cells of plants); meiosis occurs in reproductive (meiocyte) cells. (ii) Mitosis has one division producing two daughter cells; meiosis has two successive divisions producing four. (iii) Mitosis is equational – daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent; meiosis is reductional – chromosome number halves. (iv) Synapsis and crossing over are absent in mitosis but occur in prophase I of meiosis, producing genetic variation.

text: State two points of significance of meiosis.
modelAnswer: (i) Meiosis halves the chromosome number in gametes so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, conserving the specific chromosome number of each species across generations. (ii) Crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes produce genetic variation in the population, which is important for evolution.

text: A diploid organism has 2n = 24. State the number of chromosomes and DNA content (taking G₁ as 2C) in a meiocyte at (a) G₂, (b) the end of telophase I in each daughter nucleus, (c) each cell after meiosis II.
modelAnswer: (a) G₂: chromosome number 24 (each with two chromatids); DNA content 4C, since DNA doubled in S phase. (b) End of telophase I: homologues have separated, so each nucleus has 12 chromosomes (each still with two chromatids); DNA 2C. (c) After meiosis II: sister chromatids separate, so each cell has 12 chromosomes, each a single chromatid; DNA 1C.

text: Define water potential. What is its value for pure water?
modelAnswer: Water potential (Ψw) is the potential energy of water per unit volume relative to pure water, a measure of the tendency of water to move; water moves from higher to lower Ψw. It is expressed in pressure units (pascals or MPa). Pure water at standard temperature and atmospheric pressure has a water potential of zero.

text: Explain plasmolysis. How is it reversed?
modelAnswer: When a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution (lower water potential outside), water moves out by exosmosis, first from the cytoplasm and then from the vacuole. The protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall; this is plasmolysis (incipient plasmolysis when it first begins to detach). The space between wall and protoplast fills with the external solution as the wall is freely permeable. If the plasmolysed cell is placed in a hypotonic solution or water, water enters, the protoplast swells and presses against the wall again; this recovery is deplasmolysis.

text: A cell has solute potential −1.2 MPa and pressure potential 0.5 MPa. It is placed in pure water. Calculate its water potential and state the direction of water movement.
modelAnswer: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp = −1.2 MPa + 0.5 MPa = −0.7 MPa. Pure water has Ψw = 0 MPa, which is higher than −0.7 MPa. Water moves from higher to lower water potential, so water will enter the cell (endosmosis) until it becomes fully turgid and Ψw of the cell reaches zero.

text: Explain the cohesion–tension theory of ascent of sap. What are its supporting features?
modelAnswer: Transpiration from leaf mesophyll cells lowers the water potential in leaves; water is drawn from xylem into mesophyll and evaporates through stomata. This creates a negative pressure (tension) in the xylem vessels of leaves, pulling water up. Water forms a continuous column from roots to leaves because of: (i) cohesion – mutual attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding; (ii) adhesion – attraction of water molecules to the polar surfaces of xylem walls (tracheary elements); (iii) high surface tension. The narrow diameter of tracheary elements supports capillarity. The pull generated at the top is transmitted down the column to the roots, drawing water in from the soil. Supporting features: water has high tensile strength; xylem vessels are dead, narrow and lignified, preventing collapse under tension; the rate of upward flow corresponds with transpiration rate; trees shrink in diameter during intense transpiration. Up to about 15 m per hour can be achieved; root pressure contributes only a small push.
keyPoints: Continuous water column in narrow xylem

text: Distinguish between transpiration and guttation.
modelAnswer: Transpiration is evaporative loss of water as vapour from aerial parts, mostly through stomata; it occurs mainly in the day. Guttation is loss of liquid water containing dissolved salts through hydathodes at leaf tips and margins, usually at night or early morning when root pressure is high and transpiration is low.

text: Describe the mechanism of opening and closing of stomata.
modelAnswer: Stomata open and close by changes in turgidity of guard cells. During opening (usually in light), K⁺ ions are actively taken into guard cells (with Cl⁻ and malate as counter-ions), lowering their water potential; water enters by osmosis and guard cells become turgid. The outer walls are thin and the inner walls (facing the pore) thick and elastic; cellulose microfibrils are oriented radially, so turgid guard cells bow outward, opening the pore. During closing, K⁺ leaves, water flows out, guard cells become flaccid and the pore closes. ABA promotes closure during water stress.
keyPoints: K⁺ influx lowers Ψ, water enters

text: What is hydroponics? State its significance.
modelAnswer: Hydroponics is the technique of growing plants in a defined nutrient solution without soil, first demonstrated by Julius von Sachs (1860). Significance: it helps identify essential elements and their deficiency symptoms, and is used commercially to produce vegetables such as tomato, seedless cucumber and lettuce.

text: Give the criteria for essentiality of an element.
modelAnswer: (i) The element must be absolutely necessary for supporting normal growth and reproduction; in its absence the plant does not complete its life cycle or set seeds. (ii) The requirement of the element must be specific and not replaceable by another element; deficiency of one element cannot be met by supplying another. (iii) The element must be directly involved in the metabolism of the plant.

text: Describe the steps of root nodule formation in leguminous plants.
modelAnswer: (1) Rhizobia multiply and colonise the surroundings of roots and attach to epidermal and root hair cells. (2) The root hairs curl and the bacteria invade them. (3) An infection thread is produced, carrying the bacteria into the cortex of the root, where they initiate nodule formation. (4) Bacteria are released from the thread into cortical cells, leading to differentiation of specialised nitrogen-fixing cells (bacteroids). (5) The nodule establishes direct vascular connection with the host for exchange of nutrients. The nodule contains all the necessary biochemical components, such as nitrogenase and leghaemoglobin. Nitrogenase catalyses N₂ + 8e⁻ + 8H⁺ + 16ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂ + 16ADP + 16Pi; leghaemoglobin is an oxygen scavenger protecting the enzyme. The ammonia formed is protonated to NH₄⁺ and assimilated into amino acids.
keyPoints: Attachment and curling of root hairs

text: Explain the nitrogen cycle briefly, naming the organisms involved.
modelAnswer: Atmospheric N₂ is fixed into ammonia by lightning/industrial processes and biologically by nitrogen-fixing prokaryotes (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Anabaena). Decomposition of organic nitrogen of dead plants and animals to ammonia is ammonification. Ammonia is oxidised to nitrite by Nitrosomonas or Nitrococcus and to nitrate by Nitrobacter (nitrification, by chemoautotrophs). Plants absorb nitrate and ammonium and assimilate them into proteins, which pass to animals. Nitrate in soil is reduced to N₂ by denitrifying bacteria like Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere.

text: Why do deficiency symptoms of nitrogen appear first in older leaves, while those of calcium appear first in younger leaves?
modelAnswer: Nitrogen is a mobile element; it is actively mobilised from older senescing leaves to younger growing parts, so deficiency shows first in older leaves. Calcium is relatively immobile, being a structural component (calcium pectate of the middle lamella), and cannot be withdrawn from older tissues, so young tissues suffer first.
keyPoints: Mobile N moves to young leaves

text: State one function each of potassium and boron in plants.
modelAnswer: Potassium maintains anion–cation balance, helps in opening and closing of stomata, activates enzymes and maintains turgidity of cells. Boron is required for uptake and utilisation of Ca²⁺, membrane functioning, pollen germination, cell elongation, cell differentiation and carbohydrate translocation.

text: Name the products of the light reaction and state where they are used.
modelAnswer: The light reaction produces ATP, NADPH and O₂. ATP and NADPH (assimilatory power) are used in the stroma for the Calvin cycle (reduction of 3-PGA to triose phosphate and regeneration of RuBP). O₂ diffuses out of the chloroplast as a by-product.
keyPoints: ATP/NADPH used in Calvin cycle in stroma

text: Distinguish between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
modelAnswer: Cyclic: only PS I is involved; electrons from P700 return to PS I via the ETC; only ATP is formed; no photolysis of water and no O₂ evolution; occurs in stroma lamellae; operates mainly when only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available. Non-cyclic: both PS II and PS I work in series (Z-scheme); electrons from water pass to NADP⁺; ATP and NADPH are formed; water is split and O₂ evolved; occurs in grana lamellae.

text: Describe the three stages of the Calvin cycle and calculate the ATP and NADPH needed to produce one glucose molecule.
modelAnswer: (1) Carboxylation: CO₂ combines with ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), catalysed by RuBisCO, forming two molecules of 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA). (2) Reduction: 3-PGA is reduced to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (triose phosphate) using 2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed. (3) Regeneration: RuBP, the CO₂ acceptor, is regenerated from triose phosphates, using 1 ATP per CO₂. Total per CO₂ = 3 ATP + 2 NADPH. For one glucose (6 CO₂) six turns are needed: ATP = 6 × 3 = 18; NADPH = 6 × 2 = 12.

text: What is photorespiration? Why does it not occur in C₄ plants?
modelAnswer: Photorespiration is the light-dependent uptake of O₂ and release of CO₂ in C₃ plants. RuBisCO has affinity for both CO₂ and O₂; at high O₂ (or low CO₂) it binds O₂ to RuBP, giving one PGA and one phosphoglycolate. Phosphoglycolate is metabolised through the chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion, releasing CO₂, with no synthesis of sugar or ATP; it is wasteful. In C₄ plants, PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ in mesophyll cells and the C₄ acid releases CO₂ in bundle sheath cells, raising the intracellular CO₂ concentration around RuBisCO. RuBisCO therefore acts as a carboxylase, minimising oxygenase activity and photorespiration.
keyPoints: C₄ concentrates CO₂ in bundle sheath

text: State Blackman's law of limiting factors.
modelAnswer: 'If a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, then its rate will be determined by the factor which is nearest to its minimal value: it is the factor which directly affects the process if its quantity is changed.' For example, at low CO₂, increasing light intensity does not raise the rate of photosynthesis because CO₂ is limiting.

text: What is Kranz anatomy?
modelAnswer: Kranz ('wreath') anatomy is the leaf anatomy of C₄ plants in which large bundle sheath cells form a ring around the vascular bundles. These cells have a large number of chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange and no intercellular spaces. Example: maize, sugarcane.

text: Define respiratory quotient. Give its value for carbohydrates and fats.
modelAnswer: Respiratory quotient (RQ) is the ratio of the volume of CO₂ evolved to the volume of O₂ consumed in respiration: RQ = CO₂ evolved / O₂ consumed. For carbohydrates RQ = 1.0 (6CO₂/6O₂) and for fats it is less than one, about 0.7 (e.g. tripalmitin 102/145 = 0.7).

text: Distinguish between aerobic respiration and fermentation.
modelAnswer: (i) Aerobic respiration uses O₂ and completely oxidises glucose to CO₂ and H₂O; fermentation occurs without O₂ and the substrate is only partially oxidised to ethanol + CO₂ (yeast) or lactic acid (muscle, bacteria). (ii) Aerobic respiration yields up to 38 ATP (36 by some counts) per glucose; fermentation yields only 2 ATP net. (iii) Aerobic respiration occurs in the cytoplasm and mitochondria; fermentation occurs only in the cytoplasm. (iv) In fermentation NADH is reoxidised to NAD⁺ slowly via the reduction of pyruvate; in aerobic respiration via the ETS.
keyPoints: O₂ use and complete vs partial oxidation

text: Calculate the net ATP yield from the complete aerobic oxidation of one molecule of glucose, showing the contribution of each stage. Assume 1 NADH = 3 ATP and 1 FADH₂ = 2 ATP.
modelAnswer: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): 4 ATP produced − 2 ATP used = 2 ATP net (substrate-level); 2 NADH → 2 × 3 = 6 ATP. Link reaction (2 pyruvate → 2 acetyl CoA): 2 NADH → 6 ATP. Krebs cycle (2 turns): 2 GTP/ATP = 2 ATP; 6 NADH → 18 ATP; 2 FADH₂ → 4 ATP. Total = 2 + 6 + 6 + 2 + 18 + 4 = 38 ATP. (In eukaryotes, if cytoplasmic NADH enters via the glycerol-phosphate shuttle as FADH₂, the yield is 36 ATP.)

text: Why is the respiratory pathway called amphibolic?
modelAnswer: Respiration is traditionally considered catabolic, but intermediates of the pathway are also used for synthesis. When fatty acids are respired they are broken down to acetyl CoA, but when the organism needs fatty acids, acetyl CoA is withdrawn from the pathway for their synthesis. Similarly, proteins are broken to amino acids that enter the pathway as pyruvate or Krebs cycle intermediates, while α-ketoglutarate and OAA can be withdrawn to synthesise amino acids. Thus the pathway is involved in both catabolism and anabolism and is better called amphibolic.
keyPoints: Fatty acid example via acetyl CoA

text: Explain the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Oxygen acts as the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor at the end of the electron transport system. It accepts electrons from cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) and combines with protons to form water. By removing electrons, it keeps the ETS running, allowing NADH and FADH₂ to be reoxidised and ATP to be synthesised by oxidative phosphorylation.

text: Name the two types of fermentation and the organisms in which they occur.
modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation – pyruvic acid is converted to ethanol and CO₂, e.g. yeast. Lactic acid fermentation – pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase, e.g. some bacteria (Lactobacillus) and animal muscle cells during oxygen deficiency.

text: Name the three phases of growth in plants.
modelAnswer: (i) Meristematic phase – cells at root and shoot apices constantly divide; cells have large nuclei and thin primary walls with abundant plasmodesmata. (ii) Phase of elongation – cells just behind the meristem show increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new wall deposition. (iii) Phase of maturation – cells attain maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications.

text: Define differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation with examples.
modelAnswer: Differentiation: cells derived from apical/cambial meristems mature to perform specific functions, e.g. tracheary elements lose their protoplasm and develop strong lignified walls. Dedifferentiation: living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide regain it, e.g. formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from parenchyma. Redifferentiation: cells produced by dedifferentiated meristems again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions, e.g. secondary xylem and cork cells.

text: Give two physiological effects each of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid.
modelAnswer: Auxins (IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D): initiate rooting in stem cuttings; promote flowering in pineapple; prevent premature fruit and leaf drop; cause apical dominance; induce parthenocarpy (tomato); 2,4-D is a weedicide; control xylem differentiation. Gibberellins (GA₃ etc.): increase stem length (sugarcane), elongate grape stalks; delay senescence; hasten malting; cause bolting in rosette plants; promote early seed production in conifers. Cytokinins (kinetin, zeatin): promote cell division; produce new leaves, chloroplasts and lateral shoots; overcome apical dominance; delay leaf senescence. Ethylene: promotes fruit ripening and respiratory climacteric; promotes senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers; breaks seed and bud dormancy; promotes root growth and root hair formation; induces flowering in mango and pineapple; causes triple response. ABA: inhibits plant growth and metabolism; inhibits seed germination; induces stomatal closure; increases stress tolerance; induces seed and bud dormancy.

text: Distinguish between arithmetic and geometric growth.
modelAnswer: Arithmetic growth: following mitosis only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates and matures; growth rate is constant; plotting size against time gives a straight line; expressed as Lₜ = L₀ + rt (e.g. root elongating at a constant rate). Geometric growth: both daughter cells continue to divide, giving an initial slow lag phase, then a rapid exponential (log) phase, and finally a stationary phase as nutrients become limited, giving a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve; exponential phase is described by W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ.
keyPoints: One vs both daughter cells divide

text: What is vernalisation? Give its significance.
modelAnswer: Vernalisation is the promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature exposure. It prevents precocious reproductive development late in the growing season and allows the plant to reach maturity before flowering. Example: winter wheat sown in autumn germinates, overwinters as small seedlings, resumes growth in spring and is harvested in mid-summer; biennials like carrot and cabbage need cold treatment.

text: A plant cell enlarges from 10 µm³ to 25 µm³ and another from 50 µm³ to 65 µm³ in the same time. Calculate the absolute and relative growth of each and comment.
modelAnswer: Cell A: absolute growth = 25 − 10 = 15 µm³; relative growth = 15/10 × 100 = 150%. Cell B: absolute growth = 65 − 50 = 15 µm³; relative growth = 15/50 × 100 = 30%. Both show the same absolute growth, but relative growth rate is much higher in cell A because it grew more in proportion to its initial size.

text: What is the dental formula of an adult human? What does it indicate?
modelAnswer: The dental formula is 2123/2123 (I 2/2, C 1/1, PM 2/2, M 3/3). It indicates the number of each type of tooth in half of the upper and half of the lower jaw: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars, giving a total of 2 × 16 = 32 teeth.

text: Describe the role of bile in digestion.
modelAnswer: Bile, secreted by liver cells and stored in the gall bladder, contains bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin), bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipids but no enzymes. Bile salts emulsify fats, breaking them into small micelles and increasing the surface area for lipase action. Bile also activates lipases. Its alkalinity helps neutralise the acidic chyme, and bile salts aid absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins.

text: Describe the digestion of proteins in the human alimentary canal.
modelAnswer: Mouth: no protein digestion. Stomach: chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which is activated to pepsin by HCl (pH ~1.8). Pepsin converts proteins into proteoses and peptones. In infants, rennin curdles milk protein (casein → paracasein) aiding digestion. Small intestine: pancreatic juice brings trypsinogen, activated by enterokinase to trypsin; trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase. Trypsin/chymotrypsin/carboxypeptidase convert proteins, proteoses and peptones to dipeptides. Intestinal juice (succus entericus) contains dipeptidases that convert dipeptides into amino acids. Amino acids are absorbed by active transport into blood capillaries of villi.

text: Explain how the absorption of fats differs from that of glucose.
modelAnswer: Glucose (and amino acids) are absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi by carrier-mediated active transport (along with Na⁺), or partly by simple/facilitated diffusion. Fatty acids and glycerol are insoluble in water; they are first incorporated into small droplets called micelles, which move into the intestinal mucosa. There they are re-formed into very small protein-coated fat globules called chylomicrons, which are transported into the lacteals (lymph vessels) of the villi and finally released into the bloodstream.
keyPoints: Glucose by active transport into blood

text: Name the gastrointestinal hormones that regulate digestion and state the role of any two.
modelAnswer: Gastrin – stimulates secretion of gastric juice and HCl. Secretin – stimulates release of water and bicarbonate ions from the pancreas. Cholecystokinin (CCK) – stimulates secretion of pancreatic enzymes and contraction of the gall bladder to release bile. Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) – inhibits gastric secretion and motility.

text: What is meant by assimilation? How do nutrients reach the tissues?
modelAnswer: Assimilation is the utilisation of absorbed substances by tissues for energy, growth and repair, making them part of the protoplasm. Absorbed glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries of the villi and reach the liver through the hepatic portal vein, then the general circulation; fats are carried via lymph into blood.

text: Define tidal volume and vital capacity.
modelAnswer: Tidal volume (TV) is the volume of air inspired or expired during normal respiration, about 500 mL. Vital capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, or breathe out after a forced inspiration: VC = ERV + TV + IRV.

text: Explain the mechanism of inspiration in humans.
modelAnswer: Inspiration occurs when the pressure inside the lungs (intra-pulmonary pressure) falls below atmospheric pressure. It is initiated by contraction of the diaphragm, which increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis. Contraction of the external intercostal muscles lifts the ribs and sternum, increasing volume in the dorso-ventral axis. The increase in thoracic volume causes a similar increase in pulmonary volume, lowering intra-pulmonary pressure, so air from outside moves into the lungs. Additional abdominal muscles can increase the strength of inspiration.

text: Describe the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in human blood. What is the significance of the oxygen dissociation curve?
modelAnswer: Oxygen: about 97% is carried by RBCs as oxyhaemoglobin and about 3% dissolved in plasma. Each haemoglobin molecule can carry up to four O₂ molecules. Binding is mainly related to pO₂; pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature also affect it. In the alveoli high pO₂, low pCO₂, lower H⁺ and lower temperature favour formation of oxyhaemoglobin; in tissues low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺ and higher temperature favour dissociation. Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of O₂ to tissues under normal conditions. CO₂: about 20–25% is carried by haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin, about 70% as bicarbonate and about 7% dissolved in plasma. In tissues, carbonic anhydrase in RBCs converts CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺; at the alveoli the reaction reverses, releasing CO₂. Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO₂ to the alveoli. Dissociation curve: a sigmoid plot of percentage saturation of haemoglobin against pO₂; it helps study the effect of factors like pCO₂ and H⁺ on O₂ binding; a right shift indicates easier unloading in tissues.

text: Given TV = 500 mL, IRV = 2500 mL, ERV = 1000 mL, RV = 1100 mL, calculate (a) inspiratory capacity, (b) vital capacity, (c) total lung capacity.
modelAnswer: (a) Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV = 500 + 2500 = 3000 mL. (b) Vital capacity = ERV + TV + IRV = 1000 + 500 + 2500 = 4000 mL. (c) Total lung capacity = VC + RV = 4000 + 1100 = 5100 mL.

text: Why is gas exchange efficient across the alveolar membrane?
modelAnswer: The diffusion membrane is very thin (less than a millimetre; made of alveolar squamous epithelium, basement substance and capillary endothelium); the total alveolar surface area is very large; there is a steep partial pressure gradient of O₂ (104 vs 40 mm Hg) and CO₂ (45 vs 40 mm Hg); CO₂ is 20–25 times more soluble than O₂.

text: Name two respiratory disorders and their causes.
modelAnswer: Asthma – difficulty in breathing causing wheezing due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles. Emphysema – chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged, reducing the respiratory surface; cigarette smoking is a major cause. Occupational disorders such as silicosis and asbestosis are caused by long exposure to dust.

text: What is the composition of blood plasma?
modelAnswer: Plasma is a straw-coloured viscous fluid forming about 55% of blood. It has 90–92% water and 6–8% proteins (fibrinogen for clotting, globulins for defence, albumins for osmotic balance). It also contains minerals (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻), glucose, amino acids, lipids, hormones and clotting factors in inactive form.

text: Describe the mechanism of blood coagulation.
modelAnswer: When an injury occurs, platelets and damaged tissues release factors that initiate a cascade of reactions. An enzyme complex, thrombokinase, is formed, which converts inactive prothrombin present in plasma into active thrombin; Ca²⁺ ions are required. Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, which forms a network of threads in which dead and damaged formed elements are trapped, forming the clot (coagulum). This prevents excessive loss of blood.

text: Describe the events of the cardiac cycle.
modelAnswer: Assume the heart is in joint diastole: all four chambers are relaxed; tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open, semilunar valves closed; blood flows from pulmonary veins and venae cavae into the atria and then the ventricles. (1) Atrial systole: the SA node generates an action potential that stimulates both atria to contract, increasing flow into the ventricles by about 30%. (2) The impulse reaches the AV node and bundle of His, spreading over the ventricles; ventricles contract (ventricular systole) and atria relax. Ventricular pressure rises, closing the AV valves (first sound 'lub'), preventing backflow. (3) As pressure rises further, semilunar valves open and blood is ejected into the pulmonary artery and aorta. (4) Ventricles relax (ventricular diastole); pressure falls, semilunar valves close (second sound 'dub'). (5) When ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure, AV valves open and blood fills the ventricles. One cycle lasts about 0.8 s; each ventricle pumps about 70 mL per beat (stroke volume); cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min.
keyPoints: Ventricular systole – AV valves close (lub), ejection
Duration 0.8 s, stroke volume, cardiac output

text: Explain double circulation and its significance.
modelAnswer: In birds and mammals, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate in the left and right sides of the heart. Pulmonary circulation: deoxygenated blood is pumped by the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, oxygenated and returned by pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Systemic circulation: the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to all body tissues, and deoxygenated blood returns through venae cavae to the right atrium. Thus blood passes twice through the heart for each complete circuit. Significance: no mixing of blood, efficient oxygen supply to tissues, and maintenance of high pressure in the systemic circuit, needed by warm-blooded animals.

text: Explain the ABO blood group system.
modelAnswer: ABO grouping is based on the presence or absence of two surface antigens, A and B, on RBCs; plasma contains natural antibodies against the absent antigen. Group A: antigen A, anti-B antibody. Group B: antigen B, anti-A. Group AB: both antigens, no antibodies (universal recipient). Group O: no antigens, both anti-A and anti-B (universal donor).
keyPoints: Antigens on RBCs, antibodies in plasma

text: Calculate the cardiac output of a person whose heart rate is 80 per minute and stroke volume 65 mL. How does exercise affect cardiac output?
modelAnswer: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 65 mL × 80 per min = 5200 mL per min = 5.2 L/min. During exercise, sympathetic nervous stimulation and adrenaline increase both the rate and the strength of ventricular contraction, so both heart rate and stroke volume rise and cardiac output increases considerably.
keyPoints: Sympathetic/adrenaline raise rate and stroke volume

text: Distinguish between ammonotelism and uricotelism with examples.
modelAnswer: Ammonotelism is the excretion of ammonia, which is highly toxic and requires large amounts of water; seen in bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects. Uricotelism is the excretion of uric acid as a pellet or paste with minimal water loss; seen in reptiles, birds, land snails and insects.

text: Describe the structure of a nephron.
modelAnswer: A nephron has two parts: the glomerulus and the renal tubule. The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries formed by the afferent arteriole (a branch of the renal artery); blood leaves through the efferent arteriole. The renal tubule begins with a double-walled cup, Bowman's capsule, enclosing the glomerulus; together they form the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle). The tubule continues as the highly coiled proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), a hairpin-shaped loop of Henle with descending and ascending limbs, and the highly coiled distal convoluted tubule (DCT). DCTs of many nephrons open into a straight collecting duct, which converges and opens into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids. The efferent arteriole forms the peritubular capillaries and the vasa recta around the tubule.

text: Explain the process of urine formation in the human kidney.
modelAnswer: Urine formation involves three processes. (1) Glomerular filtration: blood pressure forces plasma through three layers – endothelium of glomerular capillaries, basement membrane and epithelium of Bowman's capsule (podocytes with filtration slits). Almost all plasma constituents except proteins pass, forming the ultrafiltrate. GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (180 L/day). (2) Reabsorption: about 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed. In the PCT, nearly all essential nutrients, 70–80% of electrolytes and water are reabsorbed. The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water; the ascending limb is impermeable to water but reabsorbs electrolytes. Conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water occurs in the DCT; the collecting duct reabsorbs large amounts of water (under ADH) and allows passage of small amounts of urea into the medullary interstitium. (3) Tubular secretion: tubular cells secrete H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia into the filtrate, maintaining ionic and acid–base balance. The counter-current mechanism concentrates urine up to about four times the initial filtrate.
keyPoints: Reabsorption in PCT, loop, DCT, collecting duct
Tubular secretion of H⁺, K⁺, NH₃

text: Explain the role of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS).
modelAnswer: A fall in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure or GFR activates the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells to release renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I, which is further converted to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor that raises glomerular blood pressure and GFR. It also activates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which increases reabsorption of Na⁺ and water from the distal parts of the tubule, raising blood pressure and GFR. ANF from the heart acts as a check on this mechanism.
keyPoints: Renin from JGA on fall in GFR

text: What is haemodialysis? When is it needed?
modelAnswer: Haemodialysis is the artificial removal of urea and other wastes from blood using a dialysing unit (artificial kidney). Blood from a convenient artery is pumped into a dialysing unit after adding an anticoagulant (heparin); it flows through a cellophane tube surrounded by dialysing fluid of the same composition as plasma except nitrogenous wastes, so wastes diffuse out. Cleared blood is returned through a vein after adding anti-heparin. It is needed in uremia/kidney failure.

text: Describe micturition briefly.
modelAnswer: Micturition is the process of release of urine. As the urinary bladder fills and stretches, stretch receptors on its wall send signals to the CNS. The CNS sends motor messages to contract the smooth muscles of the bladder and simultaneously relax the urethral sphincter, causing release of urine. The neural mechanism is called the micturition reflex.

text: Name the three types of movement shown by cells of the human body with an example of each.
modelAnswer: Amoeboid movement – macrophages and leucocytes in blood (using pseudopodia formed by cytoplasmic streaming and microfilaments). Ciliary movement – cilia of the trachea remove dust particles; cilia in the fallopian tubes move the ovum. Muscular movement – movement of limbs, jaws, tongue by contractile muscles.

text: Describe the structure of a sarcomere.
modelAnswer: A sarcomere is the portion of a myofibril between two successive Z lines and is the functional unit of contraction. Thin actin filaments are attached to the Z line; the light band containing only actin is the I band (isotropic). Thick myosin filaments in the centre form the dark A band (anisotropic), held together by the M line. The central part of the A band not overlapped by thin filaments is the H zone. In the resting state the edges of thin filaments partially overlap the free ends of thick filaments.
keyPoints: I band – actin; A band – myosin

text: Explain the mechanism of muscle contraction by the sliding filament theory.
modelAnswer: Contraction of a muscle fibre takes place by sliding of thin filaments over thick filaments. (1) A neural signal reaching the neuromuscular junction releases acetylcholine, which generates an action potential in the sarcolemma. (2) This spreads through the muscle fibre and causes release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm. (3) Ca²⁺ binds to troponin on actin filaments, removing the masking of active sites for myosin by tropomyosin. (4) The myosin head, using energy from ATP hydrolysis (ATPase activity), binds to exposed actin sites to form a cross-bridge. (5) The cross-bridge pulls the attached actin filaments towards the centre of the A band (power stroke); Z lines are pulled inward, shortening the sarcomere. The I bands shorten and H zone disappears, while A band length is constant. (6) ADP and Pi are released; a new ATP binds and the cross-bridge breaks; the cycle of cross-bridge formation and breaking repeats. (7) When Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, actin sites are masked again and the Z lines return to their original position (relaxation).
keyPoints: Sliding: I band shortens, A constant

text: Describe the types of synovial joints with examples.
modelAnswer: Synovial joints have a fluid-filled synovial cavity between articulating surfaces and allow considerable movement. Ball and socket joint – between humerus and pectoral girdle (shoulder) or femur and acetabulum (hip). Hinge joint – knee and elbow. Pivot joint – between atlas and axis. Gliding joint – between carpals. Saddle joint – between carpal and metacarpal of thumb.

text: Distinguish between osteoporosis and arthritis.
modelAnswer: Osteoporosis is an age-related disorder characterised by decreased bone mass and increased chances of fractures; decreased levels of oestrogen is a common cause. Arthritis is inflammation of joints. Gout is a type of arthritis due to accumulation of uric acid crystals.

text: Name the bones forming the axial skeleton and give their numbers.
modelAnswer: The axial skeleton has 80 bones: skull (22 bones: 8 cranial + 14 facial), hyoid (1), ear ossicles (6), vertebral column (26), sternum (1) and ribs (24, i.e. 12 pairs). Hence 22 + 1 + 6 + 26 + 1 + 24 = 80.

text: Distinguish between myelinated and non-myelinated nerve fibres.
modelAnswer: Myelinated fibres are enveloped by Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath with gaps called nodes of Ranvier; found in spinal and cranial nerves; conduct impulses quickly by saltatory conduction. Non-myelinated fibres are enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath; commonly found in autonomous and somatic neural systems; conduct impulses more slowly.

text: Explain how a nerve impulse is generated in a neuron.
modelAnswer: At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to K⁺ and nearly impermeable to Na⁺; the Na⁺–K⁺ pump transports 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in. Hence the outer surface is positive and the inner surface negative – the membrane is polarised, with a resting potential. When a stimulus is applied at a site, the membrane becomes freely permeable to Na⁺, leading to rapid influx of Na⁺ and reversal of polarity: the outer surface becomes negative and the inner positive (depolarisation). This electrical potential difference is the action potential, or nerve impulse. Depolarisation of the adjacent site follows by current flow, so the impulse is conducted along the axon. The rise in Na⁺ permeability is short-lived; it is followed by increased K⁺ permeability, K⁺ diffuses out and resting potential is restored (repolarisation).

text: Describe the mechanism of hearing.
modelAnswer: Sound waves are collected by the external ear (pinna) and directed through the external auditory canal to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which vibrates. The vibrations are transmitted through the ear ossicles – malleus, incus and stapes – to the oval window, which they also amplify. The vibrations pass through the oval window onto the fluid of the cochlea, generating waves in the lymph. The waves induce a ripple in the basilar membrane. These movements of the basilar membrane bend the hair cells of the organ of Corti, pressing them against the tectorial membrane. As a result, nerve impulses are generated in the associated afferent neurons. The impulses are transmitted by the auditory nerves to the auditory cortex of the brain, where they are analysed and the sound is recognised.
keyPoints: Cochlear fluid waves move basilar membrane
Hair cells bend against tectorial membrane
Impulses via auditory nerve to auditory cortex

text: Explain transmission of a nerve impulse across a chemical synapse.
modelAnswer: At a chemical synapse the pre- and postsynaptic membranes are separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft. When an impulse arrives at the axon terminal, it stimulates movement of synaptic vesicles towards the membrane, where they fuse and release neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine) into the cleft. The neurotransmitters bind to specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, which opens ion channels allowing entry of ions; this can generate a new potential in the postsynaptic neuron, which may be excitatory or inhibitory.
keyPoints: Binding to receptors, ion channels open

text: State the functions of the medulla oblongata and the hypothalamus.
modelAnswer: Medulla oblongata: contains centres that control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions. Hypothalamus: contains centres that control body temperature, urge for eating and drinking; it also contains neurosecretory cells that secrete hypothalamic hormones and, with the limbic system, regulates emotions and motivation.

text: Distinguish between rods and cones.
modelAnswer: Rods contain the purplish-red protein rhodopsin (visual purple), which contains a derivative of vitamin A; they are responsible for twilight (scotopic) vision. Cones contain three types of photopigments sensitive to red, green and blue light; they are responsible for daylight (photopic) and colour vision.

text: Distinguish between endocrine and exocrine glands.
modelAnswer: Endocrine glands are ductless; they release their secretions (hormones) directly into the blood, which carries them to target organs, e.g. thyroid, pituitary. Exocrine glands have ducts and pour their secretions into ducts that carry them to a specific site, e.g. salivary glands, sweat glands. The pancreas is a mixed (heterocrine) gland.

text: Name any three hormones of the anterior pituitary and state one function of each.
modelAnswer: Growth hormone (GH) – stimulates body growth; excess in children causes gigantism. Prolactin (PRL) – regulates growth of mammary glands and milk formation. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) – stimulates synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones. ACTH – stimulates synthesis and secretion of glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex. LH and FSH (gonadotrophins) – stimulate gonadal activity; LH induces ovulation and maintains corpus luteum; FSH regulates spermatogenesis and follicle growth. MSH – acts on melanocytes to regulate skin pigmentation.

text: Describe the mechanism of hormone action.
modelAnswer: Hormones produce their effects on target tissues by binding to specific proteins called hormone receptors, located only in the target tissues. Receptors in the cell membrane are membrane-bound receptors; receptors inside the cell are intracellular (mostly nuclear) receptors. Binding forms a hormone–receptor complex, which leads to biochemical changes in the target tissue. (a) Hormones that interact with membrane-bound receptors (protein/peptide hormones such as FSH, insulin, glucagon, and amino-acid derivatives like adrenaline) normally do not enter the target cell; they generate second messengers (e.g. cyclic AMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺) which regulate cellular metabolism, producing physiological and developmental effects. (b) Hormones that interact with intracellular receptors (steroid hormones like cortisol, testosterone, oestradiol and iodothyronines like thyroid hormones) are lipid-soluble; they enter the cell and bind receptors, and the complex interacts with the genome, regulating gene expression or chromosome function. Cumulative biochemical actions result in physiological and developmental effects.
keyPoints: Steroid/thyroid hormones → intracellular receptors → gene expression

text: Explain how blood glucose is regulated by the pancreas.
modelAnswer: The endocrine pancreas (islets of Langerhans) has α-cells secreting glucagon and β-cells secreting insulin. When blood glucose rises after a meal, insulin is secreted; it acts on liver cells (hepatocytes) and adipocytes to enhance cellular glucose uptake and utilisation, and stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis), lowering blood glucose (hypoglycaemic). When blood glucose falls, glucagon is secreted; it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver and reduces cellular glucose uptake, raising blood glucose (hyperglycaemic). Prolonged hyperglycaemia leads to diabetes mellitus, associated with loss of glucose in urine and formation of ketone bodies.

text: Distinguish between cretinism and myxoedema.
modelAnswer: Both are due to hypothyroidism. Cretinism results from hypothyroidism during pregnancy or in infancy: stunted growth, mental retardation, low intelligence quotient, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. Myxoedema (adult hypothyroidism) results from hypothyroidism in adults, causing low BMR, weight gain, puffy skin and lethargy; in adult women it may cause irregular menstrual cycles.

text: Name the hormones secreted by the adrenal medulla and state their effects.
modelAnswer: The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), together called catecholamines. They are secreted rapidly during stress or emergency ('fight or flight'): they increase alertness, pupillary dilation, piloerection, sweating, heart beat, strength of heart contraction and rate of respiration; they stimulate breakdown of glycogen, raising blood glucose, and also stimulate breakdown of lipids and proteins.
